claims.text: Significant chemical short-range order in refractory high-entropy alloys suppresses lattice thermal conductivity relative to a chemically disordered solid solution of the same composition.
The proposed conductivity suppression is caused primarily by enhanced phonon scattering from SRO-induced local chemical-potential fluctuations.
SRO can reduce dislocation mobility.
MoNbTaW is a body-centered-cubic refractory high-entropy alloy capable of exhibiting SRO.
Al0.1CrCoFeNi is an example of a chemically disordered bcc refractory high-entropy alloy.
Controlled annealing or rapid quenching followed by aging can enhance SRO while avoiding long-range intermetallic-phase formation.
Phonon-phonon scattering is dominant over the stated temperature range of 300–1000 K.
SRO significantly affects phonon mean free paths between 300 K and 1000 K.
Specific chemical ordering produces local variations in atomic mass and bond stiffness that act as phonon-scattering centers.
Mo-Nb or Al-Fe pairs are examples of local atomic correlations responsible for the proposed scattering.
SRO scatters short-wavelength phonons more effectively than fully random chemical disorder.
In MoNbTaW, SRO reduces the double-kink nucleation rate associated with screw-dislocation motion.
The influence of SRO on screw-dislocation motion in MoNbTaW becomes attenuated with increasing temperature.
Lattice thermal transport is governed by phonon scattering rather than dislocation glide.
Lattice thermal conductivity decreases progressively as the degree of SRO increases.
Long-range ordering or phase separation can change the operative thermal-transport mechanism and the conductivity trend.
AlxCrCoFeNi forms a distinct intermetallic phase for x greater than 0.5.
Once a distinct phase forms, grain-boundary and phase-boundary scattering replace SRO scattering as the relevant mechanism.
The magnitude of conductivity suppression depends on the mass and elastic-property contrast of the element pairs participating in SRO.

A same-composition SRO-enhanced sample having thermal conductivity equal to or greater than the disordered control within experimental error would falsify the proposed scattering-dominated suppression.
